categories.description: How learning with rewards works day to day.

categories.title: Behaviour and welfare

categories.title: Everyday skills
categories.description: Words you’ll hear for common training goals.

terms.shortDefinition: When something the dog values follows a behaviour, making that behaviour more likely to happen again.
terms.deeperExplanation: In behavioural science, “positive” means something is added, not that it is morally good. Positive reinforcement means adding a valued consequence after a behaviour. Over time, that behaviour tends to appear more often in similar situations. It is different from negative reinforcement, which involves removing something to change behaviour.
terms.example: Your dog sits, you give them a treat they enjoy, and sitting becomes more likely next time you practise in a similar place.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: “Positive” here does not simply mean “nice”, and “negative” does not simply mean “bad”. They describe adding or removing something.

terms.shortDefinition: Anything that, when it follows a behaviour, makes that behaviour more likely in future.
terms.deeperExplanation: A reinforcer is defined by its effect on behaviour, not by what humans assume is rewarding. Food, play, sniffing, or praise can all reinforce — but only if they actually increase the behaviour for that dog in that moment.
terms.example: If praise does not change your dog’s behaviour, but a tasty treat does, the treat is acting as a reinforcer there.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: A treat offered after a behaviour is a reward attempt; it is only a reinforcer if it strengthens the behaviour over time.

terms.shortDefinition: Something you offer the dog that they are likely to value after a behaviour.
terms.deeperExplanation: Owners usually say “reward” for the pleasant thing they deliver. Trainers may also talk about reinforcers when focusing on whether behaviour actually changes. Good Dog uses “reward” in everyday instructions and introduces “reinforcer” when that distinction helps.
terms.example: After your dog turns to their name, you give a small piece of food as a reward.

terms.shortDefinition: How the reward reaches the dog — how quickly, where, and in what way.
terms.deeperExplanation: Clear delivery helps the dog connect the reward with the moment you marked. Delivering near you can build engagement; tossing away can create space. Messy or delayed delivery can confuse what earned the pay.
terms.example: You mark the glance towards you, then place the treat by your knees so your dog finishes near you.

terms.shortDefinition: A short signal that identifies the exact moment of behaviour you want to reward.
terms.deeperExplanation: An event marker bridges the gap between the behaviour and the reward. It can be a word, a click, or another consistent signal. The marker itself is not the full reward; it predicts that the reward is coming.
terms.example: The instant your dog’s bottom touches the floor, you say “Yes!”, then give a treat.

searchPhrases: the word i say when my dog does something right
terms.shortDefinition: A consistent spoken word that marks the moment you want to reward.
terms.deeperExplanation: Many owners use “Yes!” as a marker word. Say it once, at the moment of success, then deliver the reward. Avoid turning the marker into excited chatter, or it loses its pinpoint meaning.
terms.example: Your dog looks towards you; you say “Yes!” and then give a treat. You may hear trainers call this a marker word.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: The marker word is not a cue asking for a behaviour. It comments on what just happened.

terms.shortDefinition: Any consistent signal — word, click, or other cue — used as an event marker.
terms.deeperExplanation: A clicker is a common marker signal, but a spoken word works well for many households. Choose one clear signal and keep it consistent during early learning.
terms.example: Some trainers click, then treat. Others say “Yes!”, then treat. Both are marker signals when used consistently.

terms.shortDefinition: How promptly and clearly your marker and reward follow the behaviour you want.
terms.deeperExplanation: Good timing helps your dog connect the consequence with the right moment. Marking late can accidentally pay for the next thing the dog did. You do not need perfection — aim for “close enough to be clear”.
terms.example: Marking the glance towards you works better than waiting until your dog has sniffed the floor and wandered off.

searchPhrases: what i say to ask for sit
terms.shortDefinition: A signal that tells the dog a familiar behaviour may earn a reward now.
terms.deeperExplanation: A cue can be a word, gesture, or situation. It is not the behaviour itself. Teach the behaviour first so the cue has something reliable to name. Many trainers prefer “cue” to “command” because it sounds less confrontational.
terms.example: Once your dog is happily sitting for a lure, you can add the word “sit” just before they sit.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Repeating a cue louder does not usually teach understanding — it often means the setup is too hard.

terms.shortDefinition: Using something the dog wants, often food, to gently guide them into a position or movement.
terms.deeperExplanation: Luring can make early learning easy. The long-term aim is usually to reduce the lure so the dog is not dependent on seeing food in the hand. Fade the lure by rewarding after the movement without guiding every time.
terms.example: Moving a treat slowly up and back over your dog’s nose can encourage a sit. Later, try an empty-hand gesture and reward from the other hand.

terms.shortDefinition: Waiting for the dog to offer a behaviour naturally, then marking and rewarding it.
terms.deeperExplanation: Capturing is useful for behaviours dogs already do, such as a voluntary sit or a glance towards you. You do not lure or prompt — you notice, mark, and pay.
terms.example: Your dog happens to look at you; you say “Yes!” and give a treat. Looking at you starts to happen more often.

terms.shortDefinition: Building a behaviour by rewarding small steps towards the finished version.
terms.deeperExplanation: Instead of waiting for the complete behaviour, you pay for progress: looking at a mat, then stepping on it, then lying down. Raise your criteria gradually so the dog can succeed.
terms.example: For mat work, you might first reward your dog for a glance at the mat, then a step onto it, then a settle.

terms.shortDefinition: The specific standard that earns a mark and reward in this practice moment.
terms.deeperExplanation: Clear criteria keep training fair. If the plan is “any glance towards me”, do not suddenly require a long stare. When practice is hard, lower criteria rather than repeating a cue.
terms.example: Today’s criterion might be a brief look at you. Tomorrow you might wait for a slightly longer look.

searchPhrases: works at home but not outside
terms.shortDefinition: Helping a dog learn that a behaviour is useful in different places and situations.
terms.deeperExplanation: Dogs do not automatically transfer learning from the kitchen to the park. Change one thing at a time — place, distance, distraction — and keep success easy while the picture changes.
terms.example: Your dog responds to their name indoors, then you practise in the garden, then on a quiet path.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Knowing a behaviour at home does not mean they “know it everywhere”.

terms.shortDefinition: Performing a behaviour smoothly, readily, and with little hesitation in the current setup.
terms.deeperExplanation: Fluency is about ease and consistency in a known context. It is related to, but not the same as, generalisation. A dog can be fluent at home and still need help outdoors.
terms.example: Your dog sits promptly on a quiet cue in the living room, looking relaxed and sure.

terms.shortDefinition: The pattern of how often a behaviour earns a reinforcer.
terms.deeperExplanation: Early learning usually works best with frequent, clear rewards. Later, some behaviours can be maintained with less frequent pay, but cutting rewards too soon often causes confusion. Good Dog keeps early sessions generously rewarded.
terms.example: While teaching name response, you reward almost every successful turn. Later you may reward many, but not all, successful turns.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: “Random treats forever” is not a beginner rule. Build the behaviour first.

terms.shortDefinition: When something is removed after a behaviour, and that makes the behaviour more likely.
terms.deeperExplanation: Here “negative” means removal, not “bad”. Example patterns include pressure that stops when the dog complies. Good Dog focuses on positive reinforcement and does not teach pressure-based methods. Understanding the term helps you recognise advice you may hear elsewhere.
terms.example: If walking only continues after a dog stops pulling, forward motion is being used in a pressure-and-release pattern — that is not Good Dog’s approach.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Negative reinforcement is not the same as punishment, and “negative” does not mean cruel by definition — but many common uses still create discomfort Good Dog avoids.

terms.shortDefinition: The postures, movements, and signals dogs use that help us notice comfort or worry.
terms.deeperExplanation: Soft eyes, loose body, and easy movement often suggest comfort. Freezing, lip licking, yawning out of context, whale eye, or trying to leave can suggest pressure. One signal alone is not a diagnosis — look at the whole dog and the situation.
terms.example: During handling practice, your dog turns away and stiffens. You stop and make the exercise easier.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: A single yawn or shake-off does not prove a full emotional diagnosis.

terms.shortDefinition: How activated or “wound up” a dog is in the moment — from sleepy to highly excited.
terms.deeperExplanation: Learning is often easier at a moderate level of arousal. Very high arousal can make thinking and responding harder. Arousal is not the same as aggression.
terms.example: After frantic greetings at the door, your dog may struggle to settle. A calmer warm-up helps.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: High arousal is not proof that a dog intends to be aggressive.

terms.shortDefinition: A practical way of describing the point where a dog becomes too distressed, excited, or overwhelmed to respond comfortably.
terms.deeperExplanation: Trainers often say a dog is “over threshold” when they can no longer take food, hear cues, or stay loosely responsive. The useful response is usually more distance or an easier setup — not forcing the exercise. This is a practical description, not a medical diagnosis of emotion.
terms.example: If your dog cannot notice another dog and still respond to you, increase distance rather than repeating their name louder.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Threshold talk is not a precise mind-reading tool; use it to adjust difficulty kindly.

terms.shortDefinition: How much space there is between your dog and something that matters in the environment.
terms.deeperExplanation: Distance is one of the easiest ways to make practice easier. More space often lowers pressure so your dog can notice a trigger and still work with you.
terms.example: Practising recall far from a mild distraction is easier than practising right beside it.

searchPhrases: things that set my dog off
terms.shortDefinition: Something in the situation that tends to start a noticeable response from your dog.
terms.deeperExplanation: Triggers can be other dogs, sounds, visitors, or movement. Naming a trigger helps you manage distance and plan easier practice. It does not mean the dog is “naughty”.
terms.example: The doorbell may be a trigger for rushing. You practise calm pauses far from the door first.

terms.shortDefinition: Behaviours that may show a dog is finding a situation uncomfortable or conflicting.
terms.deeperExplanation: Examples people often notice include turning away, freezing, excessive sniffing, lip licking, or trying to leave. Context matters. If you see several signs, pause and simplify. Do not use a checklist to diagnose a disorder.
terms.example: During a sound exercise, your puppy freezes and looks away. You stop and make the sound quieter and further away.

terms.shortDefinition: Activities that give a dog suitable chances to explore, sniff, search, play, chew, or solve simple problems.
terms.deeperExplanation: Enrichment supports welfare in its own right. It is not only a way to tire a dog out. Choose activities your dog can enjoy safely without frustration.
terms.example: Hiding a few pieces of food in a snuffle mat for your dog to find.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Enrichment is not a substitute for addressing fear or aggression — and harder puzzles are not always kinder.

terms.shortDefinition: Changing the situation so unwanted behaviour is less likely, while you teach something better.
terms.deeperExplanation: Management reduces risk and stops the dog practising the unwanted pattern. It is not the same as teaching a new behaviour, but it often makes training possible. Examples include leads, gates, picking up shoes, or choosing quieter walking times.
terms.example: Using a baby gate so your dog cannot rush guests while you teach calmer greetings.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Management is not “giving up”. It is part of kind, practical training.

terms.shortDefinition: Management changes the setup; training teaches a new response.
terms.deeperExplanation: You often need both. Manage to keep everyone safe and prevent rehearsal, and train so the dog learns what to do instead. Good Dog’s short exercises are training; gates and distance are management.
terms.example: A long line is management for safety outdoors; rewarding a recall is training.

terms.shortDefinition: Helping a dog become less reactive to something by presenting it in a very mild, controlled way that stays comfortable.
terms.deeperExplanation: True desensitisation stays below the point where the dog struggles. It is slow on purpose. It is not flooding (forcing them to endure something scary). Serious fear work often needs a qualified professional.
terms.example: Playing a doorbell recording at a tiny volume while your dog remains relaxed, before ever raising the volume.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Pushing a dog closer “until they cope” is not desensitisation.

terms.shortDefinition: Changing how a dog feels about something by pairing it with a better outcome, usually while it stays mild enough to handle.
terms.deeperExplanation: Often combined with desensitisation: the mild trigger predicts excellent food. It is not a quick fix for aggression or panic. If your dog is deeply afraid or dangerous around a trigger, seek qualified in-person help.
terms.example: A quiet distant sound predicts a scatter of tasty food for your dog, so the sound starts to mean good news.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Counterconditioning is not the same as simply distracting a dog forever, and it is distinct from desensitisation alone.

terms.shortDefinition: Giving the dog a real chance to opt in or opt out of handling, and stopping when they say no with their body.
terms.deeperExplanation: Cooperative handling builds trust. If your dog moves away, freezes, or shows stress signals, pause. Forcing handling can create fear of touch.
terms.example: You touch the shoulder briefly, reward, and stop while your dog still looks soft and willing.

terms.shortDefinition: Time and space for a dog to return to a calmer state after excitement, worry, or hard work.
terms.deeperExplanation: After a difficult meeting or a busy session, dogs may need quiet rest before more learning. Pushing straight into harder practice can stack stress.
terms.example: After a noisy delivery at the door, you skip training and offer a calm rest on a familiar bed.

terms.shortDefinition: Coming back to you when invited.
terms.deeperExplanation: A strong recall is built by making return brilliant and easy before adding distractions. Management (leads, long lines, secure places) keeps practice safe while you train.
terms.example: You call once in a cheerful voice; your dog runs over; you celebrate with several small treats and then let them sniff again.

terms.shortDefinition: Walking with you while the lead stays soft rather than tight.
terms.deeperExplanation: Good Dog focuses on paying for soft-lead moments and keeping sessions short. We avoid pain-based equipment and pressure battles.
terms.example: You mark and reward when the lead hangs in a gentle J shape beside you.

terms.shortDefinition: Resting calmly in a place, often on a mat or bed, without constant fussing.
terms.deeperExplanation: Settling is taught with comfort and choice. It is not the same as forcing a dog to stay still through pressure.
terms.example: Your dog goes to a mat, lies down, and softens while you sit nearby and reward calm.

terms.shortDefinition: Remaining in position until released, usually for longer or with more distance than a brief wait.
terms.deeperExplanation: Good Dog starts with brief waits. A formal stay is a longer, more formal version. Build duration slowly and keep the dog comfortable.
terms.example: Your dog sits while you take one step away, then you return and reward before they move.

terms.shortDefinition: A short, calm pause before moving on.
terms.deeperExplanation: A wait is often shorter and more everyday than a formal stay. Useful at doors, kerbs, or before release to sniff.
terms.example: Your dog pauses for one second at an internal door, you mark, reward, then release with “okay”.

searchPhrases: ignore the food on the floor
terms.shortDefinition: Turning away from something instead of taking it, often for a better outcome from you.
terms.deeperExplanation: Early leave-it games should stay easy and low conflict. Dangerous items are a management problem first. Do not use leave-it games that create a fight over resources.
terms.example: Your dog looks away from a dull object under your hand and earns a better treat from your other hand.

terms.shortDefinition: Teaching a dog to release something by making the trade worthwhile.
terms.deeperExplanation: A kind swap uses a good trade rather than chasing or prising items from the mouth. If resource guarding appears, seek qualified help rather than forcing exchanges.
terms.example: You offer a tasty trade; your dog releases a toy; you praise and sometimes return the toy.

terms.shortDefinition: Your dog willingly noticing you and choosing to connect for a moment.
terms.deeperExplanation: Engagement is invited, not demanded. Soft attention games make later cues easier because your dog already finds you relevant.
terms.example: You wait; your dog glances up; you mark and reward. Glances start to happen more often.

terms.shortDefinition: Gradually practising a behaviour with more distractions, duration, or distance while keeping success likely.
terms.deeperExplanation: Proofing is planned generalisation. Change one challenge at a time. If the dog fails often, the proofing step is too big.
terms.example: After a solid name response indoors, you add a mild toy on the floor before outdoor distractions.

searchPhrases: go to mat then lie down
terms.shortDefinition: A sequence of behaviours that run together, each step leading to the next.
terms.deeperExplanation: Chains are built from fluent pieces. If a chain falls apart, strengthen the weak step rather than repeating the whole sequence. Public trainer education often covers chains after basics are solid.
terms.example: Go to mat → lie down → relax could become a short settling chain once each piece is easy.

terms.shortDefinition: Moving through doorways with a calmer, more controlled pattern.
terms.deeperExplanation: Usually built from brief waits, management, and rewarding settled feet — not from confrontation.
terms.example: Your dog pauses as the door opens a little; you mark calm, then release through.

terms.shortDefinition: Helping a dog learn where toileting is wanted, mainly through routine, supervision, and rewarding outdoor success.
terms.deeperExplanation: Housetraining is mostly management plus clear pay for toileting in the right place. Scolding accidents often teaches dogs to hide when they need to go. Sudden regression can be medical and needs a vet check.
terms.example: You take your puppy out after a nap; they wee on the grass; you calmly mark and reward, then play a little.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Accidents are rarely “spite”. They usually mean the schedule, supervision, or health picture needs adjusting.

terms.shortDefinition: Lying down on purpose when invited — elbows on the floor — without being pushed into position.
terms.deeperExplanation: A comfortable down is taught with luring or shaping, then named with a cue. It is different from a settle on a mat, though the two skills support each other. Never force hips or shoulders down.
terms.example: From a sit, you lower a treat to the floor; your dog folds into a down; you mark and reward.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: “Down” for lying down is not the same as asking a jumping dog to get “down” off a person — use clear, separate cues in everyday speech if needed.

terms.shortDefinition: When a puppy or dog puts teeth on skin or clothes during exploration or play — common in youngsters, and best handled with pauses and redirects.
terms.deeperExplanation: Mouthing is often normal puppy behaviour, especially when tired or overexcited. Useful responses include stopping play briefly, offering a toy or chew, and arranging more rest and enrichment. Painful or fearful biting, or guarding with growls and snaps, needs qualified in-person help — not an app treatment plan.
terms.example: Your puppy mouths your sleeve; you pause; you offer a soft toy; they chew the toy instead and play continues briefly.
terms.commonMisunderstanding: Smacking, shouting, or holding the mouth shut often worsens fear or rough play rather than teaching a kind alternative.
